blocks.body:
The prime number theorem for arithmetic progressions says that for a fixed modulus $q$ and $\gcd(a,q)=1$, the primes up to $x$ are shared equally among the $\varphi(q)$ admissible classes. In applications the modulus is rarely fixed. In the circle method, for instance, one needs the count of primes $p \le x$ with $p \equiv a \pmod q$ for all $q$ up to a power of $\log x$ simultaneously, with an error that is small compared with $x/\varphi(q)$.

The Siegel–Walfisz theorem (Walfisz, 1936, building on Siegel's theorem of 1935) gives exactly this: equidistribution uniformly for $q \le (\log x)^A$, for any fixed $A$, with an error saving a factor $e^{-c\sqrt{\log x}}$. It has a price: because it relies on [[siegel-zeros|Siegel's theorem]], the implied constant cannot be computed.

blocks.title: ψ(x; q, a)
blocks.body:
For $\gcd(a,q)=1$,
$$\psi(x;q,a) = \sum_{\substack{n \le x \\ n \equiv a \ (q)}}\Lambda(n),$$
where $\Lambda$ is the von Mangoldt function ($\Lambda(p^k) = \log p$, and $0$ on non-prime-powers). It counts primes $p \equiv a \pmod q$ up to $x$ with weight $\log p$, plus a negligible contribution $O(\sqrt x\log x)$ from higher prime powers; its expected size is $x/\varphi(q)$.

blocks.title: Reduction to characters and zeros
blocks.body:
Orthogonality of characters gives
$$\psi(x;q,a) = \frac{1}{\varphi(q)}\sum_{\chi \bmod q}\overline\chi(a)\,\psi(x,\chi),\qquad \psi(x,\chi) = \sum_{n\le x}\chi(n)\Lambda(n).$$
For the principal character, $\psi(x,\chi_0)$ differs from $\psi(x)$ only by the prime powers dividing $q$, at most $O(\log q\log x)$, and the prime number theorem with the classical error term (see [[pnt]]) gives $\psi(x) = x + O(xe^{-c\sqrt{\log x}})$. So the task is to show that $\psi(x,\chi)$ is small for each $\chi \ne \chi_0$.

The [[explicit-formula]] expresses $\psi(x,\chi)$ through the zeros $\rho = \beta + i\gamma$ of $L(s,\chi)$. For a primitive non-principal $\chi$ modulo $q$ and $2 \le T \le \sqrt x$,
$$\psi(x,\chi) = -\sum_{|\gamma| \le T}\frac{x^\rho}{\rho} + O\Bigl(\frac{x\log^2(qx)}{T}\Bigr),$$
and passing to an imprimitive character changes $\psi(x,\chi)$ by $O(\log^2(qx))$. Each zero contributes $|x^\rho| = x^\beta$, so what matters is how far the zeros stay from the line $\beta = 1$.

The [[zero-free-region]] says that, apart from at most one exceptional real zero $\beta_1$ belonging to a real character $\chi_1$, all zeros with $|\gamma| \le T$ satisfy $\beta \le 1 - c/\log(qT)$. There are $O(T\log(qT))$ zeros up to height $T$. Take $T = e^{\sqrt{\log x}}$ and $q \le T$. A non-exceptional zero then contributes at most
$$x^{\beta} \le x\exp\Bigl(-\frac{c\log x}{\log(qT)}\Bigr) \le x\exp\Bigl(-\frac{c}{2}\sqrt{\log x}\Bigr),$$
and the truncation error is $O(xe^{-\sqrt{\log x}}\log^2 x)$. Balancing the two losses is what produces $\sqrt{\log x}$ in the exponent. Carrying this out carefully (Davenport, Chapter 20) gives the following.

blocks.title: Prime number theorem for progressions, first form
blocks.body:
There are absolute constants $c, c_1>0$ such that for $q \le \exp(c_1\sqrt{\log x})$ and $\gcd(a,q)=1$,
$$\psi(x;q,a) = \frac{x}{\varphi(q)} - \frac{\overline{\chi_1}(a)\,x^{\beta_1}}{\varphi(q)\,\beta_1} + O\bigl(x\,e^{-c\sqrt{\log x}}\bigr),$$
where the middle term is present only if some real character $\chi_1$ modulo $q$ has an exceptional zero $\beta_1$. Everything here, including the constants, is effective. (Proof omitted.)

blocks.title: The Siegel–Walfisz theorem
blocks.body:
For every $A>0$ there is a constant $C_A$ such that for all $x \ge 2$, all $q \le (\log x)^A$ and all $a$ with $\gcd(a,q)=1$,
$$\psi(x; q, a) = \frac{x}{\varphi(q)} + O_A\bigl(x\, e^{-c\sqrt{\log x}}\bigr),$$
that is, the error is at most $C_A\,x\,e^{-c\sqrt{\log x}}$, where $c>0$ is absolute. The constant $C_A$ is ineffective.

blocks.title: Proof from the first form and Siegel's theorem
blocks.body:
For $x$ larger than some $x_0(A)$ we have $(\log x)^A \le \exp(c_1\sqrt{\log x})$, so the first form applies; smaller $x$ can be absorbed into $C_A$. It remains to show that the exceptional term is small.

The zero $\beta_1$ belongs to a real character $\chi_1$ modulo $q$, induced by a primitive real character modulo some $q^* \mid q$, and $L(s,\chi_1)$ and $L(s,\chi_1^*)$ have the same zeros in $0<\sigma<1$. Siegel's theorem with $\varepsilon = 1/(4A)$ gives
$$1 - \beta_1 \ \ge\ c(\varepsilon)\,(q^*)^{-\varepsilon} \ \ge\ c(\varepsilon)\,q^{-1/(4A)} \ \ge\ c(\varepsilon)\,(\log x)^{-1/4}.$$
Since $\beta_1 > 1 - c/\log q$, we may assume $\beta_1 \ge \frac12$ (shrinking the absolute constant $c$ of the zero-free region if necessary). Hence
$$\frac{x^{\beta_1}}{\varphi(q)\beta_1} \le 2x\exp\bigl(-(1-\beta_1)\log x\bigr) \le 2x\exp\bigl(-c(\varepsilon)(\log x)^{3/4}\bigr).$$
Since $(\log x)^{3/4}$ grows faster than $\sqrt{\log x}$, there is a constant $C'_A$ with $\exp(-c(\varepsilon)(\log x)^{3/4}) \le C'_A\exp(-c\sqrt{\log x})$ for all $x \ge 2$. This proves the theorem. The constant $C'_A$ depends on $c(\varepsilon)$, which Siegel's theorem does not let us compute.

The choice $\varepsilon = 1/(4A)$ rather than $1/(2A)$ keeps the constant $c$ in the exponent absolute: with $\varepsilon = 1/(2A)$ one would get $\exp(-c(\varepsilon)\sqrt{\log x})$, with an unknown constant in the exponent.

blocks.title: Equivalent forms and the limits of the range
blocks.body:
By partial summation the theorem is equivalent to
$$\pi(x;q,a) = \frac{\operatorname{li}(x)}{\varphi(q)} + O_A\bigl(x\,e^{-c'\sqrt{\log x}}\bigr)\qquad (q \le (\log x)^A),$$
where $\pi(x;q,a)$ counts primes $p \le x$ with $p \equiv a \pmod q$. A weaker form that is often quoted, and is all that many applications need, is: for all $A, B > 0$,
$$\psi(x;q,a) = \frac{x}{\varphi(q)} + O_{A,B}\Bigl(\frac{x}{(\log x)^B}\Bigr)\qquad(q \le (\log x)^A).$$

Why only powers of $\log x$? Suppose $q$ is as large as $x^\delta$. Siegel's bound then only says $1 - \beta_1 \ge c(\varepsilon)x^{-\delta\varepsilon}$, and $x^{\beta_1 - 1} \le \exp(-c(\varepsilon)x^{-\delta\varepsilon}\log x)$, which does not tend to $0$. A possible exceptional zero could then make the term $x^{\beta_1}/\varphi(q)$ as large as the main term. Three other results fill in different parts of the picture.

1. Under [[grh]], $\psi(x;q,a) = x/\varphi(q) + O(\sqrt x\log^2 x)$ for all $q \le x$, which is non-trivial up to $q \le x^{1/2-\varepsilon}$.
2. The [[bombieri-vinogradov]] theorem gives an error of GRH quality on average over $q \le x^{1/2}(\log x)^{-B}$. Its proof uses Siegel–Walfisz for small moduli and the large sieve for the rest.
3. Upper bounds of the correct order hold for all $q < x$: this is the Brun–Titchmarsh inequality from [[selberg-sieve]].

blocks.title: Primes modulo 7 up to a million
blocks.body: Compute $\psi(10^6;7,a)$ and $\pi(10^6;7,a)$ for $a = 1,\dots,6$ and compare them with the predictions $10^6/6$ and $\operatorname{li}(10^6)/6$.
blocks.solution:
A direct computation gives
- $\psi(10^6;7,a) \approx 166560.3,\ 166518.7,\ 166676.6,\ 166586.3,\ 166683.2,\ 166547.9$ for $a = 1,\dots,6$, against $10^6/6 \approx 166666.7$. The largest deviation is about $148$ (at $a=2$), well below $\sqrt{10^6} = 1000$.
- $\pi(10^6;7,a) = 13063,\ 13065,\ 13105,\ 13069,\ 13105,\ 13090$, which together with the prime $7$ itself add up to $\pi(10^6) = 78498$. The prediction is $\operatorname{li}(10^6)/6 \approx 13104.6$.

Deviations of size about $\sqrt x$ are what GRH predicts. Siegel–Walfisz guarantees much less, an error $O(xe^{-c\sqrt{\log x}})$ with an unknown constant, but it does so uniformly in $q \le (\log x)^A$. A single numerical table can neither confirm nor refute an ineffective asymptotic statement.

blocks.title: The least prime in a progression
blocks.body: Let $p(q,a)$ be the least prime $p \equiv a \pmod q$. Deduce from the Siegel–Walfisz theorem that for every $\varepsilon > 0$, $p(q,a) \le \exp(q^{\varepsilon})$ for all $q \ge q_0(\varepsilon)$ and all $a$ coprime to $q$. Is the threshold $q_0(\varepsilon)$ computable?
blocks.solution:
Let $A = 1/\varepsilon$ and $x = \exp(q^{\varepsilon})$, so that $q = (\log x)^A$ and the theorem applies. Higher prime powers $p^k \le x$ with $k \ge 2$ contribute at most $O(\sqrt x\log^2 x)$ to $\psi(x;q,a)$. So the contribution of primes is at least
$$\frac{x}{\varphi(q)} - C_Ax\,e^{-c\sqrt{\log x}} - O(\sqrt x\log^2x) \ \ge\ \frac{x}{q}\Bigl(1 - C_Aq\,e^{-c\,q^{\varepsilon/2}}\Bigr) - O(\sqrt x\log^2 x),$$
using $\sqrt{\log x} = q^{\varepsilon/2}$. The bracket tends to $1$ as $q \to \infty$, and $\sqrt x\log^2 x$ is negligible against $x/q$ because $x = \exp(q^\varepsilon)$ grows much faster than any power of $q$. So for $q \ge q_0(\varepsilon)$ there is a prime $p \le x$ with $p \equiv a \pmod q$.

Since $C_A$ is ineffective, so is $q_0(\varepsilon)$. This bound is very weak: Linnik (1944) proved, by quite different methods, that $p(q,a) \le C q^{L}$ for absolute, effectively computable constants $C$ and $L$. In practice the least prime is much smaller still; for every $2 \le q \le 300$ and every $a$ coprime to $q$ one finds $p(q,a) < q^2$, the worst ratio $p(q,a)/q^2$ being $7/9$ at $q=3$, $a=1$.

blocks.body:
- The hypothesis $\gcd(a,q)=1$ is required.
- Ineffectivity is real: from Siegel–Walfisz alone one cannot extract an explicit $x_0$ beyond which, say, every progression modulo $q \le \log x$ contains a prime up to $x$. Results that need explicit thresholds (such as explicit forms of the three-primes theorem) must treat the possible exceptional zero separately.
- The range $q \le (\log x)^A$ is tiny. Most sieve applications need moduli up to a power of $x$, which is why [[bombieri-vinogradov]] is needed.
- The two constants play different roles: $c$ in the exponent is absolute, while the implied constant depends on $A$ and is ineffective.
- Relative to the main term the error is $\varphi(q)\,e^{-c\sqrt{\log x}} \le (\log x)^Ae^{-c\sqrt{\log x}}$, which tends to $0$; outside the range no such conclusion follows.

In Vinogradov's proof of the [[ternary-goldbach]] theorem by the [[circle-method]], the major arcs require exactly the distribution of primes in progressions to moduli up to a power of $\log x$, which Siegel–Walfisz supplies. In the [[bombieri-vinogradov]] theorem it handles the small moduli, and it appears as the standard hypothesis ("the sequence satisfies a Siegel–Walfisz condition") in many results on bilinear forms and sieves. An exclusion of Siegel zeros ([[no-siegel]]) would make these results effective and would extend the range of uniformity.

1. Deduce from the theorem that $\psi(x;q,a) = x/\varphi(q) + O_{A,B}(x(\log x)^{-B})$ for $q \le (\log x)^A$.
2. Show that $\pi(x;q,a) \sim \pi(x)/\varphi(q)$ as $x \to \infty$, uniformly for $q \le (\log x)^A$ and $\gcd(a,q)=1$.
3. In the proof, what goes wrong if Siegel's theorem is replaced by the effective bound $1-\beta_1 \gg q^{-1/2}(\log q)^{-2}$? For which range of $q$ does the argument still work?
4. Assuming GRH, for which $q$ (as a function of $x$) does the bound $O(\sqrt x\log^2 x)$ still imply $\psi(x;q,a) \sim x/\varphi(q)$?
